query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Sn to a single-phase fcc FeCoNi high‐entropy alloy will induce a nano‐scale formation of a second (BCC) phase or precipitates that pin magnetic domain walls, thereby increasing the coercive field above the typical ~100 Oe measured for the pure fcc phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi (or derived HEAs) known for high saturation magnetization but low coercivity (<100 Oe).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor addition of Sn (on the order of a few atomic percent) into the FeCoNi-based alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be synthesized under standard conditions (e.g., arc-melting followed by appropriate annealing) that have been validated for obtaining single-phase fcc structures, with processing parameters adjusted to favor the emergence of a nano-scale second phase upon Sn addition.
generation.structural_mediator: The Sn addition is expected to destabilize the pure fcc phase, prompting the nucleation of nano-scale BCC regions or Sn-induced precipitates within the fcc matrix that serve as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
generation.mechanism: By promoting a partial phase transformation or precipitation of a structurally distinct phase, the added Sn increases local magnetic anisotropy and creates interfaces that impede domain wall motion. This pinning effect enhances the coercivity compared to the homogeneous fcc matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a coercive field significantly higher than ~100 Oe, while maintaining high saturation magnetization. The presence of the secondary phase or nano-precipitates will be detectable by X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its similar derivatives with coercivity ≤100 Oe.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys processed under conditions that normally yield a single-phase fcc structure. The intervention is limited to compositional modifications (Sn addition) and does not involve altering processing methods such as severe deformation or multi-step heat treatments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Sn required and the resulting volume fraction and morphology of the induced secondary phase are uncertain. It is also not fully clear how the microstructural evolution will balance increased coercivity with possible changes in saturation magnetization and other magnetic properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of FeCoNi-based HEA samples with incremental Sn additions (e.g., 0, 2, 5, and 10 atomic percent) using arc-melting and standardized annealing protocols. Characterize the phase constitution using X-ray diffraction and TEM to detect the presence of any secondary (BCC) phases or precipitates. Perform magnetic hysteresis measurements (e.g., via vibrating sample magnetometry) to extract coercivity and saturation magnetization values.
measurements: X-ray diffraction peaks and TEM images to observe phase separation or nanostructural features
Magnetic hysteresis loops to measure coercive field values
Comparison of saturation magnetization to check for trade-offs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-added samples do not show clear evidence of a nano-scale secondary phase (or precipitates) that correlates with a statistically significant increase in coercivity (e.g., an increase of more than 50% over the baseline sample) despite similar processing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work exhibits the effects of Sn addition on the magnetic properties and microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The results show all the samples consist of a mixed structure of face-centered-cubic (FCC) phase and body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix. It also shows that the Curie temperatures (Tc) of the FCC phase and the saturation magnetization (Ms) of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs increase greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The thermomagnetic curves indicate that the phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K. This work provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperatures.

In this work, the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc-melt casting. Effects of Sn content on the phase constitution and magnetic properties were studied. All the samples are composed of FCC and BCC phases, whereas some unknown phases appear with the addition of Sn. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nanoprecipitates in the BCC matrix. Moreover, the Ms increases greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases with the increasing of x for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs. The addition of Sn can obviously increase the Curie temperature of the FCC phase. The phase of alloys with a mixture of FCC and BCC will transform from FCC to BCC phase at high temperature, leading to an increase of magnetization. They can be used as new soft magnetic materials at high temperatures.
